caption:
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says it is "quite terrible" that so much of the world's limited DRAM sits inside personal computers.
On the Cheeky Pint YouTube show, he said that memory is used about 5% of the time and belongs in the cloud.
It lands in the middle of a memory shortage: IDC says PC shipments fell 20.1% in the third quarter.

Should memory go to your PC or to AI data centers?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Tom's Hardware, Windows Central · Photo: Getty Images, G.Skill, Micron, HotHardware

image.generate: The man in the first image, in a plain dark sweater, stands on top of a huge messy heap of thousands of desktop computer RAM memory sticks that spills across the floor of a dim data center aisle, server racks on both sides. He holds one memory stick up in his hand and looks at it with a calm, serious expression. Open gaming PC towers with their side panels removed lie on the floor at the bottom of the heap. On the server rack wall behind him hangs a big metal panel with the logo from the second image, big and exact, black on white. Harsh cold fluorescent light, cables hanging, slightly cluttered and real. The exaggerated mountain of memory sticks makes the scene clearly symbolic. Blank surfaces, no readable text or labels on any object, memory stick or rack apart from the logo. Generous headroom above the man's head. The man and the logo fill the upper two thirds of the frame, the heap fills the bottom third. Photorealistic, high contrast, vertical composition, one clear subject, no letters, no watermarks. It must look like an unedited real photo from a news agency, not a painting, not digital art, no glow effects.

site_article.headline: Sam Altman says PC memory is a poor use of the world's limited DRAM supply
site_article.dek: The OpenAI chief argued that memory in home computers sits mostly idle and would do more work in cloud data centers, as a global shortage lifts device prices.
site_article.summary: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it is "quite terrible" for people to keep large amounts of the world's limited DRAM in their own computers. He said that memory is used about 5% of the time and would be better used in the cloud.
site_article.seo_title: Sam Altman calls PC RAM a poor use of scarce DRAM supply
site_article.seo_description: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman says DRAM in home PCs sits idle most of the time and belongs in the cloud, as a memory shortage pushes up prices.
site_article.answer_summary: Altman said that from a global allocation view, memory in personal computers is used only about 5% of the time, so scarce DRAM would be better used at full capacity in cloud data centers.
site_article.hero_alt: Sam Altman delivering remarks at a conference.

paragraphs.text: OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman said it is "quite terrible" for people to keep large amounts of the world's limited DRAM supply in their own computers, according to remarks reported by Tom's Hardware on October 30, 2026. He made the comments in an interview with the YouTube channel Cheeky Pint.

Altman framed the issue as a question of global allocation. He said memory in personal computers is used only about 5% of the time, and that in a supply-constrained market the goal should be maximum utilization in the cloud. He added that many people's intuition runs the other way.

Tom's Hardware reported that the remarks were aimed at local inference, the practice of running AI models on a person's own machine rather than on remote servers. Running models locally requires large amounts of memory, and a typical desktop today carries around 32GB of RAM, the outlet noted.

Both Tom's Hardware and Notebookcheck pointed out that OpenAI's main business is closed models that run in data centers and are sold through subscriptions and cloud services. Notebookcheck added that Altman's argument leaves out the other everyday uses of PC memory, such as gaming, regular applications and multitasking.

Windows Central linked the comments to earlier statements in which Altman described a future where intelligence is sold like a utility, with people buying it on a meter. The outlet also said Microsoft acknowledged RAM supply issues when it reported its latest Xbox results.
A market already short on memory

The comments arrive during a prolonged memory shortage. Micron reported revenue of $54.23 billion for its quarter ended September 3, 2026, and chief executive Sanjay Mehrotra said demand will exceed supply in both 2027 and 2028, according to The Next Web. About 75% of Micron's 2027 memory output is already committed, and AI and server customers receive priority allocation.

The shortage is showing up in consumer prices. Raspberry Pi raised the price of its 2GB Pi 4 from $35 to $67.50, citing memory costs, and Samsung added $100 to most of its Galaxy S26 range, The Next Web reported.

PC sales have also fallen. Worldwide PC shipments dropped 20.1% year over year in the third quarter of 2026 to 62.7 million units, according to preliminary IDC data reported by HotHardware. IDC pointed to early stockpiling ahead of price increases, ongoing component shortages and higher retail prices, and said the next few quarters could get worse before they improve.

Altman's argument is an efficiency case for pooling a scarce resource where it can be kept busy around the clock. It also matches the business model of the company he runs, which sells access to models hosted in data centers. For buyers already paying more for laptops, phones and memory upgrades, the remarks put a sharp point on who gets priority when supply is tight.
Watch whether memory prices for PCs and phones keep rising into 2027, as Micron's outlook suggests, and whether AI companies push harder to move everyday computing into the cloud.
